03 / Field guide

Understand how each language works.

Architecture changes what a result means. Expand a technical brief to inspect the programming model, adoption cost, integration boundary and known limitations.

Bend: architecture, tradeoffs and coexistence

Technical architecture

Bend’s guide describes a pure, affine, dependently typed language with explicit IO. It documents native CPU and GPU execution, while its JavaScript target runs parallel calls sequentially. Bend pairs laws with proof definitions; the negative fixture we inspected rejects an unfinished claim used as a proof. Kujo provides runtime execution and type diagnostics. Spec, Eval and Workcell are separate tools that check other parts of the workflow.

When to choose Bend

Evaluate Bend when you can state the central requirement precisely and prove it within the supported language subset. Its guide emphasizes proof construction and balanced parallel computation. This can suit mathematical invariants, but you will need to learn its affine programming model, write explicit annotations and maintain the proofs.

Can you use both?

You could place a Bend component behind a process or file interface and check the surrounding workflow with other tools. We did not test a Kujo–Bend adapter. Keep proof results separate from integration tests: a proof about the component does not show that the application calls it correctly.

Honest limitations

Bend excludes unsafe and foreign code from its stronger proof verdict. Its guide also says that translation into the small kernel is not itself proven. Kujo’s output checks cover the assertions and runs you define, rather than every possible input. In either case, review whether the specification expresses the requirement fully.

Reviewed baseline: Website v2.0.37; source 64230dcb96f2da2cc5a44524e42d5eb34771a6ec. Full comparison and sources ↗

BAML: architecture, tradeoffs and coexistence

Technical architecture

The BAML source we reviewed contains a compiler, a check command that collects project diagnostics and a test command that runs compiled test sets. Its current website describes typed AI functions, concurrency and tracing. These claims do not establish a speed advantage over Kujo. Kujo handles language execution in its runtime and provides task contracts and run records through separately versioned tools.

When to choose BAML

Consider BAML when you need typed AI functions within an existing application. Its quickstart and language bridges offer a starting point for adding one component at a time. Before choosing a bridge, check the supported host language, runtime version and data types.

Can you use both?

You could connect BAML application code to Kujo workflow tools through a process or service interface. We did not test a direct Kujo bridge, and support for another host language does not imply Kujo support. Define a versioned request/response format and test how failures cross the interface.

Honest limitations

Current BAML material and older structured-output DSL tutorials may describe different generations. Choose a release or source commit before copying examples. Kujo’s separate tools also need configuration and vary in maturity. Type checking and successful parsing constrain data structure; they do not show that an AI answer is true or meets a business requirement.

Reviewed baseline: Source 648ad5ed10f543c129b51789c7d02e29b64f06f7; release API observed baml-language-0.22.3-nightly.20261018.a (not runtime-tested). Full comparison and sources ↗

Zero: architecture, tradeoffs and coexistence

Technical architecture

Zero’s installation guide documents interpreter, native JIT, native executable and C++ output modes. It distinguishes the WebAssembly browser compiler from support for native libraries and code generation. We did not reproduce these capabilities locally. Kujo’s inspected CLI supports VM and interpreter execution with optional JIT paths; its workflow tools do not change the language’s memory model.

When to choose Zero

Try Zero’s preview if its documented value semantics and systems behavior suit your workload. Explore the browser examples, then establish source access, platform support and release policy before depending on it. Resource cleanup and concurrency behavior may matter more to your application than agent-workflow tools.

Can you use both?

A process or file interface could connect the languages, but we did not test a Kujo–Zero integration. First identify a repeatable Zero toolchain, then check its exit codes, data formats and native-library interfaces.

Honest limitations

Without a verified source repository or release version, we cannot independently assess Zero’s implementation, security boundaries or maturity. Kujo’s evidence tools also require configuration and meaningful checks. Deterministic cleanup alone does not make network responses or builds repeatable, or create an auditable agent run.

Reviewed baseline: Developer preview; numbered release not verified. Full comparison and sources ↗

04 / Field guide

Where Kujo’s toolchain fits.

Kujo is a language with separately versioned workflow tools. This is a possible composition, not an automatic pipeline installed with the language.

  1. 01

    Specify

    Spec

    Write observable acceptance criteria.

    A valid task record can still describe an incomplete requirement.
  2. 02

    Check

    Eval

    Evaluate files and command outcomes.

    A passing assertion covers that assertion, not every possible input.
  3. 03

    Execute

    Workcell

    Configure an execution boundary and retain receipts.

    A normal language process is not automatically sandboxed.
  4. 04

    Record

    RunLedger

    Connect supplied results to commands and Git context.

    A recorded pass verdict is not an independent correctness proof.
  5. 05

    Review

    ShipCheck

    Bring release-readiness signals to the decision.

    A human or explicitly authorized gate still owns the release.

To check agent-written code, define what success requires and run checks that test those requirements. Follow the verification workflow ↗

05 / Field guide

Check that the verifier rejects an incorrect result.

A useful verifier must reject a known failure. This small artifact exercise makes that distinction observable.

Kujo 1.8.2 computes a value. A separate Python checker parses the JSON and requires the integer 42. Wrong values, malformed JSON, missing fields and wrong types must fail.

This is one deterministic artifact check—not a coding-agent evaluation, proof of arbitrary software, or cross-language performance benchmark.

Read the method and run it locally ↗
01 / Producer · Kujo 1.8.2
print(to_json({"total": 6 * 7}))
02 / Independent checker · Python 3
{"total": 42}ACCEPTRequired value and type
{"total": 41}REJECTKnown wrong-value control
{"total": "42"}REJECTWrong type, even if it looks right

The receipt records the runtime version, command results and source/output hashes. This single run does not establish performance.

01 / Decision guide

AI-native programming languages: a practical comparison

AI-native describes a design goal, not a safety certification. Compare what each language helps an agent do, which mistakes its tools can reject and what evidence you can inspect after a run. The right choice depends on your application and the guarantees it needs.

Read the guide ↗02 / Decision guide

Programming languages for AI agents: choosing the host and tools

Choose an agent’s host language by the tools it must call, the permissions those tools need and the failures it must recover from. The host coordinates the agent; the repository it edits can use another language. Test the interfaces between them before deciding whether any language change is needed.

Read the guide ↗03 / Decision guide

AI code verification tools: what each check can establish

Use independent checks tied to clear requirements to verify AI-generated code. A type checker rejects some invalid programs, a test checks selected behavior, and a proof establishes a stated property within its assumptions. An execution record helps show what ran. Build your verification process around the facts you need each tool to establish.

Read the guide ↗04 / Practical walkthrough

Verify agent workflows: contracts, checks and reproducible evidence

Check an agent’s completion report against the work it produced. Define the requirement first, inspect the output with an independent checker and keep the commands, results and environment details needed to repeat the check. This guide shows how to connect those steps using a small runnable example.

Read the guide ↗
